title: Notes of Ministry - 82 - September 1979

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 82 - September (2494)/Notes of Ministry - 82 - Septem - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I had in mind to say something as to how God uses individuals, and therefore I have read about these four persons—Nehemiah, Rhoda, Paul’s sister’s son, and Mary of Magdala. God is able to accomplish things through individuals. There is one thing that stands entirely by itself—the great work of redemption was accomplished by one Man, Jesus Christ. It was taken up on behalf of the whole human race and accomplished by one Man who Himself came in and dealt with the devastation on the race. There was one Man only who, perfect in His obedience, was able to accomplish the work of redemption, to glorify God in it, and give God a basis to bless. That is how we as believers have come into blessing, through the work of the one Man Jesus Christ. I trust He has become endeared to every heart here, the one Man Jesus Christ who has wrought the work that provides for our eternal blessing and our blessing even now. That great work stands by itself, stands in all its glory, in all its uniqueness; there could be no other, no other saviour, no other lord, than the Man Christ Jesus.

Then I think that God, as He proceeds in His ways in the testimony, may call upon any one of us to stand in a certain situation at any given moment. The question is, would we be ready for it? Would we be prepared to stand in a situation as if everything depended on us, depended on me or depended on you? in another sense, of course, God does not need us; He could do without us; but the way He operates is largely through human vessels. God would take up someone to stand in the breach and to hold the position that He has in mind.

Now Nehemiah was a man like that. He lived in a day when the saints had been taken into captivity, when the walls of Jerusalem were in ruins, and when he got a message that those who were still there were under great affliction and learned about the state of Jerusalem, his feelings came into expression. He mourned and wept and was in great sadness and in prayer.

That has happened in the recovery. The truth of the assembly was recovered largely through the faithfulness of a man. The other side is that God works in His sovereignty; but from Nehemiah’s standpoint I think we see recovery brought about through the faithfulness of one man.

I wanted to apply this scripture to how things work out in local assemblies. If there is any expression of the truth of the assembly in our localities, dear brethren, I think in some sense it has to come down to the faithfulness of someone who is with God, feeling the breakdown that exists, and concerned to see something emerge that is according to the divine thought. So Nehemiah went down and looked at Jerusalem; he went round it in detail. Think of someone in our localities looking around to see the present state and condition of things in the testimony and feeling it with God. Nehemiah went round the different parts and viewed the wall of Jerusalem. He says, “but I told no man what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem”. The man who typically had light as to the assembly had it in his heart, not only in his mind but in his heart, he was a man who had a heart for Jerusalem. God can use such a man in relation to local assemblies. It would afford pleasure to God to see in local assemblies territory held for Christ. That is one thing that a local assembly means, that there is a bit of

territory down here held for the heart of Christ; God can find pleasure in that. As there are a few believers who want to go on in the light of the assembly, that means something to God, and it means something to Christ, to look down on a certain place and see that.

I think heaven would be looking on as Nehemiah went forward with these exercises. He looks around and then the question arises in the presence of failure and breakdown—how is the situation going to be met? What is the answer to it? What Nehemiah came to was—“Come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach”. What is needed is separation from evil, and separation from the world. That is the only way something can be secured in our places for God, some real answer to the light of the assembly—build up the wall of Jerusalem. The enemy will be against that. Later in the book certain ones sent saying,

“Come, let us meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono”, (Nehemiah 6: 2). ‘Let us come and see if we can take some common ground. Let us have an interdenominational meeting; we know we have differences of opinion and doctrine, and differences of practice, but let us find some common ground’. Is that the way? With Nehemiah it was not; he had the divine thought in his mind that the securing of the truth of the assembly is by way of the rebuilding of the wall.

The principles of separation from evil and separation from the world are essential in a day of breakdown and confusion. It is the way out of it. Four times it says they came after this manner; Nehemiah says, I am doing a great work and cannot come down (Nehemiah 6: 3).
You have a positive work before you, a work according to the mind of God where the confusion is. You build up the wall; it must start with the great principle of separation

from evil. You cannot have the work of God and the world all mixed up; they just will not mix; you cannot arrive at the divine thought that way. You have to maintain the divine thought, and if God has someone around who has Jerusalem in his heart, who has the assembly in his heart, and is committed to this great thought of rebuilding the wall, insisting on the principles and practice of separation, then you can start; you have the means for reaching practically in the present day the great divine idea of the assembly.

Now Rhoda is a younger person, she is called a maid. I would like to encourage our young people that they may have a part in what the Lord has brought them into. We have been brought into an area where He wants us to have part in things. This was a difficult time in the testimony. James had been slain; Peter had been put in prison and he was just about to be taken out to gratify the expectation of the people. Then at that point God intervenes. It says,

“but unceasing prayer was made by the assembly to God concerning him” (Acts 12: 5). Peter was released and comes along to this house, “the house of Mary, the mother of John whose surname was Mark, where were many gathered together and praying. And when he had knocked at the door of the entry, a maid came to listen, by name Rhoda”.

It would appear that, although they were praying, there was an unbelieving condition there. It is a very sobering thing to think of. It was right to make prayer in the matter, but there was unbelief operating and that is what makes Rhoda so important at this point. Someone could discern the voice of Peter. She must have had some previous knowledge of the voice of Peter.

It is a great matter to get experience of the voice of the Lord’s servants so that you know that voice, because the situation may arise where you cannot hear it any longer. She would probably not have heard it in the prison. Peter was not free then, but as he comes to the door she recognises his voice. It is a good thing to be going on with divine things in the ordinary experiences of your soul, just in your ordinary everyday experience, because there may arise a time, a critical time, when your experience will stand you in good stead.

So she recognises the voice of Peter. It is not worthless you see to go on day by day reading the Scriptures, listening to and reading ministry, praying and having to do with the Lord; these are not worthless pursuits; some time, dear young brother or sister, that experience will stand you in good stead. So she recognised the voice of Peter, but she was not the door keeper, she was not there to open the door. We need to be careful what we open the door to; but she ran in and reported that Peter was at the entry. The others said, “Thou art mad”. Well, you have sometimes got to be prepared to be misunderstood, but though you are misunderstood, if you know something stand by it. It is not very flattering when the local brethren in their unbelief turn round and say to a young sister who is bringing them the answer to what they were praying about, ‘You are mad’. They said, “It is his angel”, but she maintained that it was Peter.

However, they come to it; “Peter continued knocking: and having opened, they saw him and were astonished”. Dear brethren, we want to be realistic about our prayers; we pray, but then let us look for the answers; let us not be casual and go away and forget what we have prayed about. We come to the prayer meeting on Monday evening; will we remember on Tuesday evening what we were praying about on Monday evening, will we be looking for some answer, and continue looking? Let us be with the
Lord not only in praying but in following up our prayers in exercise looking for the answer.

Then not only should we pray but we should give thanks too. I think the reality of thankfulness comes as we see these answers coming, and our hearts go out to God in gratefulness for them. So Rhoda was the link at this time. The company were praying, but unbelieving, but Rhoda was the vital link. Now, dear young sister, could you stand in a situation like this and be the vital link, with your ear, you might say, in tune with the voice of Peter? Then we find that the brethren are coming round to see and accept that the Lord is working.
Now Paul’s sister’s son is also very interesting. Here again it is a young person, he is a youth.

The previous night the Lord had told Paul that as he had borne testimony in Jerusalem so he must bear witness at Rome also (Acts 23: 11). You might say, Well, things are perfectly sure in the Lord’s mind; He has told Paul what He is going to do and therefore He is perfectly committed to it. Quite so, the Lord is able to carry things through, but then He is pleased to use someone as an instrument to do it, to see that what He has in mind will be effected. That is where Paul’s sister’s son came in. So you get this banding together of these Jews with a murderous intent against Paul who at this point was the distinctive vessel of the testimony.

We are in days marked by the combinations of men, and some of our young people are having to stand on their own feet and give testimony to their conscience in the face of these combinations of men. I wonder how you would act if you had to stand up at one of those tribunals and be a witness and give testimony as to your own conscience.

Well, I think this youth put his life at risk. It reminds us of the spirit of Christ in Esther; she said, “and if I perish, I perish” (see Esther 4: 16), and I think it was the same spirit which was active in this youth at this point. So he came and reported the matter to Paul, and Paul was able to have it brought to the notice of the chiliarch.

The youth is brought to the chiliarch to explain what he had discovered; he finds there is a certain element of sympathy there, and it works out for the salvation of Paul from the murderous intent of this combination of men. Now the Lord used this youth, dear young brother. If you were in a situation like that could the Lord use you? This youth would have known Paul; he would have loved Paul; and the way he acts would be in keeping with that.

So it is a great thing to develop an affectionate link with those who are older in the testimony than you are, for a moment may come when the Lord wants to use you to stand in some breach in the testimony.

Now Mary in John 20 is somewhat different; she is one who could get a vital communication because she was there to receive it. The other disciples had gone to their own homes but she remained at the tomb. What held her there? Affection for Christ. She was a woman with affection for Christ and she stayed there. Well, you say, it was not a very intelligent thing because the tomb was empty; but that was the last place in which she knew He was and she remained’ there out of affection for Him—“They have taken away my Lord”. Do you have that affectionate link with Christ that would hold you at the last point where you knew He had been? Affection for Christ, that is what Mary represents. Think of the personal way she speaks. It is not just the Lord that the brethren knew, it is ‘ my Lord’, and she speaks of Him later as Rabboni, my own Teacher. It is that link with Christ that Mary had which is, so essential; it is to be in the fibre of our beings, and not only in the sisters. I have taken up Mary because she represents what the Lord can do with a woman. Mary had her own distinctive place, and at this point she could take up this situation when the others had gone home.

Now the Lord comes to her and He gives her this distinctive message for His brethren, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. What a message for a sister to get! The Lord was indicating that He was going, you might say, immediately. Oh the wealth of relationship that that would open up to us—“My Father and your Father”; the saints are to be brought into that relationship; “and to my God and your God”. The declaration of God is there in its fulness and the Lord is giving this message saying He is ascending. Well, that is very fine and Mary comes and conveys it to the company. I think that in this there is something of the spirit of the assembly working.

It reminds me of what the Lord would communicate to us in a word at the Supper in the service of God. It says she “comes bringing word to the disciples that she had seen the Lord”; it is “bringing word”. That delightful, informal way is, you might say, the spirit of the assembly working. It is the informal way in which the Lord would convey something, and a brother stands up and conveys the thing informally in a family setting. It is not formal teaching; that has its place and there are brothers fitted for that kind of service, but then, are we available as the Lord might indicate something, just to bring word to the disciples, to communicate simply what the Lord has in mind? Sisters have their own place in being able to convey something, privately, but then I think it would include us all, that we might be available in affection for the Lord. At the moment when He has something to communicate there is someone there to communicate it. Oh to be in that situation, just to be available!

Well, that is simply, dear brethren, what I had in mind; there are times when God will use an individual in a particular way and the thing is to go on steadily in ordinary exercises so that when the occasion arises we are ready for it.

I suggest putting these scriptures together, beloved brethren, in connection with the Lord awaking out of sleep. It may be that some, or many, of us are in measure troubled as to the conditions prevailing among the saints. It says in connection with this violent gust of wind that Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. I would desire for myself, and for my brethren, the ability to keep an eye upon the Lord Jesus in this position, both eyes indeed!

There is no storm in the testimony that the Lord does not know about, and there is no storm or gust of wind either which takes Him by surprise, but one would covet the ability to learn from Jesus in this restful position. Evidently, from what the Lord said, it was a lack of faith which led to the fearfulness; that is, perhaps, there was not a sufficient appropriation of Him and His attitude. But it was real, very real, to have the Lord asleep in the boat and such a violent gust of wind to come down. Yet the Lord would have us, I believe, fix our attention upon Him, His movement, or His waiting without movement for the moment, so far as specific action in the matter is concerned.

Not that I am suggesting that the Lord is ever inactive, but here on this occasion He was asleep. How touching it is to think of the Lord of glory in this position, the One who Himself said, “The Son of man has not where he may lay his head”, Matthew 8: 20.

I suppose the occasion of this crossing was one of the few opportunities that the Lord had for sleep. How touching it is to think of the lowliness of the circumstances, the sacrificial way in which Jesus was here, yet no doubt this scene teaches us that no matter what storm may arise, no matter how Satan’s power in adversity may seem to be about to overwhelm, the Lord is in the position where His own are and a view of Him, beloved, will cause us to be restful. No doubt we shall each, in every experience in the testimony, have to search ourselves as to our faith, and the Lord would raise such a question with us, but the impression that is gained is of the greatness of His Person. How wonderful to be increased in our souls, beloved, in a deep sense of the greatness of the Person of Jesus! He is able for every squall of wind, from whatever direction it comes.

The reference in Psalm 78 is, I realise, not a direct reference to the Lord Jesus waking out of sleep, because it is a simile, “as one out of sleep”, but it does say that “the Lord awoke”, and it is in my mind, beloved brethren, that there may be certain conditions among the saints which cause the Lord grief. There are things in this psalm which are referred to as forsaken or rejected, rejected by God. I think we each need to learn what God will reject and to reject those things ourselves. Then at least one of the references to what is rejected involved the movement of God’s sovereignty in a majestic way, so that we also have to make way for the sovereign actions of God at any time. But there are statements in this psalm which refer to conditions among the children of Israel, and show that the conditions which arose provoked God’s anger and moved Him to jealousy (Psalm 78: 58).

I would like to convey an impression as to the feelings of God about the conditions among His people. There is nothing, however small it may seem to us, as to the conduct of the saints or our part in the assembly, or in our relations with one another, which is not of great interest to God, because God’s dwelling is among His people and the conditions among His people are, therefore, of the greatest interest to Him. One would raise the challenge as to whether there is any tendency with us to forsake the divine standard of the truth as it has been set out for us, any turning away from the heavenly character of our testimony, involving the dignity and glory of sonship being in expression in our walk here; any suggestion of association with the world around us, or the taking on of worldly features and conduct. I think that God feels these things, and if they should in any sense tend to creep in amongst us one would raise the challenge as to God’s claims, because as I say, His dwelling is among His people. It says “God heard” (Psalm 78: 59). I think we could say also, God sees.

So I would speak feelingly as to this reference to “the tent where he had dwelt among men”, because God greatly values suitable conditions among His people for His own dwelling. He says elsewhere, “I went about in a tent and in a tabernacle”, 2 Samuel 7: 6. Beloved brethren, God will have conditions that are suitable to Him, and if there is anything, any feature of the world it may be, which we find we are tending to take on, let us feel with God about it, let us reject it, and let us think about His claims in view of His dwelling-place among His people.

Conditions must be holy, beloved, as we find later in this reference to the building of His sanctuary like the heights. True conditions for the divine dwelling involve elevation, what is morally above this world, and what is holy too, His sanctuary.

As to this reference to the Lord awaking as one out of sleep, I would suggest that the Lord may at any time act in a sudden way. Let us not be found out, beloved brethren, by our links in any direction being not according to His mind. It says that He “awoke as one out of sleep, like a mighty man that shouteth aloud by reason of wine; And he smote his adversaries in the hinder part, and put them to everlasting reproach”. Satan is the source of worldly influences that would draw us away from devotion to Christ and the assembly, and we can count upon the Lord being ready at any time to intervene. I think there is a suggestion of an intervention from an unexpected quarter. He smote them in the hinder part and put them to everlasting reproach, and then there is His choosing the tribe of Judah, “the mount Zion which he loved; And he built his sanctuary like the heights, like the earth which he hath founded for ever”. I had not any more to say about this passage, except to refer to the great importance in God’s sight of the spiritual and heavenly conditions required among the saints for His dwelling.

In the scripture in Genesis, which is well known to the brethren, one simply suggests that we might have a view of what is before the Lord Jesus. This scripture refers to Him typically as having been into death, and we can think of the view that the man would have of the woman as he woke from the deep sleep—“This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh: this shall be called Woman, because this was taken out of a man”. Beloved, the Lord Jesus has the assembly before Him. He delivered Himself up for it, as Paul tells us (Ephesians 5: 25), and the thoughts of Jesus were immediately in the direction of the assembly as He was raised from the dead. He refers to Mary as “woman” in John 20, and then uses her personal name also, and one would desire that we might increasingly have before us the greatness of the Lord’s thoughts as to the assembly, what He has before Him. There is nothing second-rate at all in the Lord’s view, beloved brethren, nothing substitute. It is the assembly that He has in mind, and we are to have in view what He desires; we are to have it before us. It is the assembly in its fulness which the Lord Jesus has in view. He had it before Him in going into death, and the distinctiveness of the assembly as a vessel answering to Himself comes out in this scripture. “This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”; there is accord with Himself in the assembly, and that in a formative way; that is, that the woman was formed out of the man.

One would bring this before the saints in simplicity as giving us a view of the ideal that the Lord has before Him, the assembly in its perfection as answering to His own heart. This, I believe, would be the answer to any flagging of devotion on the part of any one of us, as one feels it is often on one’s own part, and no doubt others feel the same. But think of the Lord Jesus having the assembly in its glory continually in His thoughts. He gave Himself for it, and His activity in nourishing and cherishing and the washing of water by the word all has in view that the assembly should be secured as a vessel entirely for Himself, for His enjoyment and pleasure and, beloved brethren, we are to have our part in it. Through grace we have been called to that, and we are to be exercised, I believe, as to the moral features which contribute to the state of conformity to Christ which will answer to Himself, as set forth in this scripture, which typifies the assembly as a vessel for His pleasure. May the Lord graciously put these thoughts together in a way which will be of some value to the saints, but in view of His own pleasure in the assembly, and God’s pleasure as dwelling among His people, for His name’s sake.

It might be helpful to look at the Lord Jesus as our Shepherd, and Psalm 23 suggests itself as presenting Him in this character. This beautiful psalm is perhaps so well known generally that much of its precious detail is lost sight of. It is written in the singular and is the outcome of soul experience. One can think of David leading the sheep and chanting this psalm as thoughts of his great Antitype—Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep—filled his soul.
David’s very pathway and occupation thus produce a yield for God.

Of all the Psalms this one is perhaps the best known. It is called a “Psalm of David”, but it may be learned and sung by each one of us as having known and proved the Lord Jesus as our Shepherd. It does not speak of His official greatness; it bespeaks His heart—what He is and what He does! It is helpful to note the position of the psalm, coming between the abandonment and work of Christ on the cross (Psalm 22) and His millennial glory (Psalm 24). In Psalm 22 there is “the voice of a man”. He is abandoned—suffering for sin from God.

But He is heard, and a threefold circle of responsive affection is secured for God as a result of His work. In Psalm 24 we get the Lord taking His place as King of glory, but Psalm 23 speaks of the same blessed Person known here on earth in every circumstance through which the believer has to pass.

Psalm 22 gives us the good Shepherd laying down His life for the sheep; Psalm 23, the great Shepherd tending and feeding the sheep; Psalm 24 the chief Shepherd seen in exaltation and glory. He will shepherd the nations in that day.

Now if I say “The Lord is my shepherd”, it involves that I am His sheep, and that I am submissive and my will is not in exercise. Such an expression is not to be a beautiful sentiment but a reality: and then what is the effect? “I shall not want”. Often difficulties and trials beset and hinder us, but this word admits of no doubt; “I shall not want”. Now I am free to come under the compulsion and leading of love. “He maketh me to lie down ... he leadeth me ...”. He would have me restful before Him. “My meditation of Him shall be sweet”.

Meditation and prayer are preferable to study—and greater in results. I am at rest in green pastures. In His alluring grace He compels me to lie down—He maketh me. Then He leadeth me beside the still waters. It is all to the end that I may learn Himself. Mary placed herself, in a submissive spirit, at His disposal, and she was led beside still waters. Martha forgot the Shepherd, for she said, “dost thou not care?” Of course He cared, but His delight at that moment lay in leading Mary into rest to hear His word (Luke 10: 38–42). We need to cultivate this kind of abstraction.
Note the shepherd care of Jesus as He said to His disciples after their arduous service, “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place and rest a

little. For those coming and those going were many, and they had not leisure even to eat”, Mark 6: 31. He is going to feed them according to the integrity of His heart and He is guiding them by the skilfulness of His hands (Psalm 78: 72).

He leads us in that He may lead us out. “He restoreth my soul”, the weariness and pressure of the way are lost sight of, and He leads out now in testimony—the paths of righteousness for His name’s sake. Our service manward is poor and unworthy if we have not first been restful with Christ. Our Shepherd is sensitive to all that is not consistent with the paths of righteousness. Let us be simple about this—Jesus is our Shepherd; He is set for our good and prosperity. He serves not for wages but in love; what a contrast to the sheep master (2 Kings 3: 4) or the sheep shearer (1 Samuel 25: 2). The false shepherds in Ezekiel 34 served for wages; they ate the fat and clothed themselves with the wool. We have a Shepherd who loves to feed His flock and to strengthen the weak. He knows every sheep and its distinguishing feature. A brother showed me a shepherd on his farm who had the care of four hundred sheep and lambs, and he said the shepherd knew every one because of certain marks, and could tell which were missing. I thought of our Shepherd as having tended and succoured myriads of sheep and knowing each one severally because He had died for each.

Shepherd instincts and care contribute to promotion amongst the saints and also to their prosperity. God took David from the sheepfolds, from following the ewes great with young, and made him to be the leader of His people. There are two features with a shepherd—he can follow the sheep and he can lead. Following has a generation in view, but leading is to promote the knowledge of the heart of God and the mind of Christ. “He leadeth
me beside the still waters” and would there make divine thoughts known to me. What a Shepherd He is! Nothing can alarm the sheep if they are near Him—if straying they are exposed to danger.
‘In His presence we are happy,
In His presence we’re secure’.

His eyes are upon the sheep. How He follows the movements of the man in John 9 and eventually leads him into the flock. Forsaken of parents, despised by neighbours, cast out by the religious leaders, he is found by Jesus. Surely he would say, “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want”. Then in John 10 he finds green pastures.

A sheep either follows or strays. A sick sheep gets away alone, and we have seen such, alas! a brother or sister who nurses a grievance and keeps away from the brethren. We need the features of our great Shepherd to recover such. “He leadeth me”. People say, ‘I am so easily led’, they usually mean led in a wrong direction. Why not let Him lead? Under such leading (Psalm 23: 4) I can “walk through the valley of the shadow of death” without fear. The same One who lay in the dust of death in Psalm 22 now supports me even in death’s valley. But it is only the shadow of death. I am no longer held in bondage. The One who shepherds me through has become the Lord even of death. The enemy would discourage us with the shadow of death, but he has been robbed of the substance by the Lord, who says, “Fear not ... I ... have the keys of death and of hades”, Revelation 1: 17, 18. The public testimony of verse 3 may be followed by persecution, trial, even death (as in v.4), as suffering for righteousness, but before the pressure comes He has calmed my soul beside the still waters.

I met an ungodly soldier in France—a lad of 19—and I asked if He had a Christian mother. He said, ‘Yes’. Then I asked what she had told him to read in times of difficulty and danger, and he said, ‘Something about the valley of the shadow of death’, but he did not know where it was. We sat down together in the presence of about two hundred wicked men and read this psalm. A day or two after he confessed Christ, and a few weeks later was killed in battle. He had gained the knowledge of the Shepherd who would sustain him even in the valley of the shadow of death.

This verse has been a comfort to many; but what about “thy rod and thy staff”, His control over me and His support for me? They go together and the psalmist speaks in the plural now, “they comfort me”. Would we covet the staff without the rod? We can know His support only as being controlled by Him. Comfort follows obedience and “His commandments are not grievous”.
“Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies”. What a triumph! A table
‘furnished’ even on earth. Thus He would set us up in power and as nourished by Himself.

“Thou hast anointed my head with oil”. Are we true to the oil? If so, the effect is seen. “My cup runneth over”. There is now the overflowing of what has been enjoyed inwardly. Do not let us be stoical or seek to suppress spiritual emotions. We have an outlet for these, to God first and then to man. Many of us lack the simplicity which the true knowledge of God would give us.

Now the Psalmist reaches a most blessed conclusion. “Surely goodness and loving-kindness shall follow me all the days of my life”. So all is well, past, present, and future, all in the hands of our great Shepherd. We can ‘praise Him for all that is past’, but there is more; we can ‘trust Him for all that’s to come’. Jacob could speak of “The God that shepherded me all my life long to this day” (Genesis 48: 15), and he could look on to the future whilst blessing the sons of Joseph. ‘Surely goodness and loving-kindness shall follow me”, there is no doubt now as to the future.

After this psalm is known we can claim the whole earth for the Lord (Psalm 24). The Shepherd of Psalm 23 is none less than the King of glory. Do our hearts rise to it now? All power is in His hands and we look on to the day when He shall have His rightful place; meanwhile how comforting is His service to us. ‘We love the Shepherd’s voice’; “He calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out”, but never into a place where He cannot go with them, for “He goeth before them”. The results of His shepherd care were seen in Peter, how jealously the Lord looked on him. He is ultimately commissioned to “shepherd my sheep” and his work and his epistles show how true he was to that commission. Then as having imbibed the spirit of his Master he desires a succession of shepherds, not in name but in character (1 Peter 5). Peter exhorts the elders to shepherd the flock of God. Paul counsels the elders at Miletus to shepherd the assembly of God. Both Peter and Paul had learned from the good Shepherd how to shepherd the saints. Both alike, too, could desire that shepherding be continued amongst the people of God, and this can only be as we learn Christ as the good Shepherd, the great Shepherd, and the chief Shepherd.

The good Shepherd gave His life for the sheep (John 10: 11). The great Shepherd is a risen Christ tending His own on earth (Hebrews 13: 20). The chief Shepherd waits to reward every faithful under-shepherd (1 Peter 5: 4).
(Jottings from a reading, date and place unknown. Some quotations are from the Authorised Version).
Thy voice, our God, in purpose we have heard,
Exalting Christ Thy well beloved Son—
‘It is not good for man to be alone’,
Th’assembly as His helpmate now is known.
We answer to Thy ways in discipline
To purify ourselves in love for Christ,
From that which claims but honours not His name,
Thus find rejection, loneliness, and shame.
We thank Thee, as we follow in this path
Of righteousness and faith and love and peace,
For others too who call upon the Lord
With willing hearts and answer to His word.
Thus true assembly feelings now are found
In moral features suited to our Lord;
The Spirit’s universal triumph seen
In hearts who on their Head together lean.
Melbourne, 19

“BE NOT CONFORMED TO THIS WORLD”—This is Paul’s word in Romans 12: 2, and we need to let it have its full weight with us. It bears on every part of our lives. It is a reproach to a christian to be indistinguishable from a worldly person. As the Lord says in John 17: 11, we are “in the world”, but we no more belong to it than Christ did. He says, “They are not of the world, as I am not of the world”. Let us therefore not take on its colour, its habits, its manners, its amusements. Again, the Lord says in John 14: 19, “If ye were of the world, the world would love its own”. How sad it is if the world begins to look upon us as “its own”, going along in its course.

But there is a triumphantly positive side. Far from being conformed to this world, we are, says Paul, to be transformed by the renewing of our mind. God is now before us. It means that we are in the path in which Jesus walked when here. He lived wholly in the Father’s will, delighting in it. What a privilege to walk here “as he walked” (1 John 2: 6). He the object of our renewed minds so that, by the Holy Spirit, we are transformed and take on something of Christ’s character as attached to Him, the centre of another world. So we are to take on heavenly colour and character as our minds are happily subject to the will of God, proving how good that will is as our lives are increasingly controlled by it.

Has sin shown itself in our walk? Far from undergoing the misfortune of remaining under the effect of our sin, we experience through the intercession of Jesus that gracious help, which sets us again before God, perhaps broken-hearted, still before God to whom we confess our sin. Our confession of sin is made to God, not to Jesus in order that He may intercede. His intercession on our behalf always goes on; it precedes us in our return to God. Therefore John does not say, If any man repent, we have an advocate; but he says, “If any man sin”, for repentance in us is itself the result of the intercession of Jesus.
paragraphs.source: J. N. Darby (‘Coll. Wrtgs.’ Vol. 28, p.308)

paragraphs.text: God goes on with His people in holiness, not passing over any sin as a light matter, but securing, not only that it should have been judged once for all in the death of Christ, but also that it should be measured morally in the light of that death, and rightly felt about in priestly exercise before Him. One would earnestly desire that more priestly ability to take up things in this way were found amongst the people of God. It is often easier for us to burn the sin-offering than to eat it. See Leviticus 10: 16–18. That is, to act in a judicial spirit rather than to make the sin our own before God, as did Ezra, Nehemiah, and Daniel. (See Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, Daniel 9).
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (‘Outline of Leviticus’, p.83)

paragraphs.text: There is this wonderful thing in Scripture that, as you are in communion and read it, you can actually feel yourself in company with the Lord, and hear Him speak; you can say, I have heard His words. John’s gospel and the epistles to Timothy are just what are attacked by the enemy in the present day, because they are the very scriptures suited to help us in it. The gospel was written after 2 Timothy.

Now one great help to this accuracy is this—never present anything, however clearly you may see it, if you have not reached it for yourself. I have found that many a thing which I had presented in an extreme way because I was sure of it, I put forth in a simpler and more real way when I had touched it in my own experience.
paragraphs.source: J. B. Stoney (‘Letters to Labourers’, p.38)

paragraphs.text: When Aaron met Moses on the mount of God he kissed him; Aaron had the love. Moses had the light and Aaron had the love; these two must always be combined, they must never be divorced; the light and the love are indissolubly in our Apostle and High Priest, and are they not to be combined in the priestly family? Are we to be content with light without the love?
We shall be, unless we use the water; unless the flesh is dealt with unsparingly, we shall not have the love ...

The dispensation is going on in life and we want to get the good of what has been carried down by those still living and apply the things and bring God into them and see if there may not be restoration, recoveries, additions and increase amongst us, which I believe will go on to the end.
It is a great mistake to confound between the light which a servant may bring and the work of God. You get the light through an instrument, but it is God who makes the light effective.
